thread.title: Becoming a caregiver for an older adult
thread.title_full: Becoming a caregiver for an older adult

author: C. G. Horn
title: Becoming a caregiver for an older adult
text:
Caregiving can be both rewarding and overwhelming, according to a May 13 statement from clinical social services coordinator Shelby Greene. Greene said, “There is a spectrum of sentiment when it comes to caregiving. On one end are folks who are overwhelmed, stressed and uncertain of their new role. On the other are people who feel it is a great honor to care for another and are resilient. Both are OK and neither deserves judgment.”
More than 41 million caregivers were estimated to be caring for loved ones aged 50 and older in the United States in 2020, an increase from previous years as reported by studies from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Caregiving tasks may include helping with daily activities such as bathing, dressing, managing medications, providing transportation to medical appointments, or managing household responsibilities.
Leslie Baker, director of geriatric pharmacy services, said that communication is essential: “We typically see caregivers when they are already in the thick of caregiving. These are four ideas we discuss with those care partners,” Baker said. “First is communication, followed by discussing what is realistic, adjusting your role and, lastly, acceptance.” Greene added that communication should also continue throughout the relationship to set expectations and goals: “Sometimes the wish of the one being cared for becomes the wish of the caregiver and that is not always realistic… If you delegate tasks or take on help, it is not a reflection of your love for them.”
Baker highlighted challenges related to expectations: “Our current societal structure is not set up to care for older adults who require more assistance… Many I have spoken with believe Medicare will provide everything they need when they are older and that is simply not the case.” Discussions about what care can realistically be provided may help clarify roles within families.
Changing roles can affect relationships between caregivers and their loved ones. Greene said boundaries can help navigate these changes: “Find what you as a caregiver are capable of doing… This is an ongoing conversation.” Acceptance also plays an important part; Greene noted that independent adults retain authority over their own decisions if they remain sound of mind: “You can be there; you can listen; but if your older loved one decides on a course of action… that is their decision.”
Resources mentioned include Alzheimer’s Association support groups for those caring for individuals with dementia or Alzheimer’s disease; Nevada Caregivers website offering documents and local service links; Powerful Tools for Caregivers workshops provided by Sanford Center for Aging; and Sanford Assessment health reviews offered free by Sanford Center.
